title: COIDA — Organisational Injury and Disease Claim Process Flow
subtitle: Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993, as amended by Act 10 of 2022, and the 2026 Regulations · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells an employer what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment an employee is injured or an occupational disease is diagnosed until the claim closes and lessons feed back into controls. It covers reporting, temporary disablement pay, rehabilitation and return to work, incapacity, and the new inspection and penalty regime.

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: COIDA as amended by the COID Amendment Act 10 of 2022 is the binding law. Proclamation Notice 306 of 2026 (GG 53990, 23 January 2026) brought most of the Amendment Act into operation on 23 January 2026; sections 3 to 6 (governance of the Fund) on 1 February 2026; and the provisions listed in paragraph (c), which are the administrative-penalty provisions, on 1 April 2026. Section 1(g) (the new “earnings” definition) and part of section 1(h) (exclusions from “employee”) are not yet in operation. Four sets of regulations were published in GG 54273 of 6 March 2026 and took effect on publication: Prescription (R.7205), Chapter XA Inspection, Compliance and Enforcement, Rehabilitation, Reintegration and Return-to-Work (“RRR Regs”), and Registration of Third Parties. Section numbers below are those of the principal Act as amended, not of the Amendment Act.

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: Act = COIDA as amended; binding now.
Reg = the 2026 Regulations or other subordinate law (including OHS Act regulations); binding now.
Code = Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294, in effect 4 September 2025). Not a statute, but anyone applying the LRA must take it into account.
BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt as policy so it becomes binding internally.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: Internal targets are set inside every statutory limit, and the clock starts on the day any supervisor or manager learns of the accident or disease, not the day the COIDA Administrator hears of it. Where it is unclear whether a matter is reportable, the flow reports it and lets the Commissioner decide liability.

notes.heading: Five interpretation points that shape the flow
points: Counting days. COIDA does not say business or calendar days. Under the Interpretation Act 33 of 1957 s.4, “days” are calendar days, excluding the first day and including the last, unless the last day is a Sunday or public holiday. Diarise in calendar days. Section 39(1) runs from the employer “having received notice” of the accident “or having learned thereof in some other manner”; knowledge of a supervisor is very likely to be treated as the employer’s knowledge.

Twelve months or three years. Substituted s.44 now says the right to benefits lapses if the accident is not brought to the Commissioner’s attention within three years. Notice to the employer no longer stops the clock; only notice to the Commissioner does. But s.43, of which only the heading was amended, still requires a claim to be lodged within 12 months. The Prescription Regulations (reg 2(3)) say claims reported under ss.38, 39, 43, 44 and 65 prescribe three years after the accident, diagnosis or treatment under s.73(3). Plan to the 12-month window; never tell an employee a claim is out of time. That is the Commissioner’s decision.

Which penalty regime applies. The administrative penalties in ss.39(6), 39(8), 40(4), 47(3)(c), 64, 81(3), 83(6) and 87 replace criminal offences (s.99), but paragraph (c) of the Proclamation only brought them into force on 1 April 2026, and its cross-references are ambiguous. For failures on or after 1 April 2026, assume the new penalties apply. The 10% penalties do not say whether the base is the earnings of all employees or of the injured employee only; take legal advice before paying one.

Accident or disease. “Accident” now means an incident or occurrence arising out of and in the course of the employee’s employment and resulting in personal injury, illness, occupational disease or death, and “occupational disease” expressly includes post-traumatic stress disorder. Accidents must be reported within 7 days (s.39(1)); diseases within 14 days (s.68(2)), “irrespective of whether” the employer thinks the disease was contracted in its employ. Where a condition follows a traumatic incident, or the category is unclear, report as an accident within 7 days and flag the disease.

Who is the employer. A temporary employment service (TES) is the employer of the workers it places (s.1 “employer” (c)). A sub-contractor’s unregistered employees are deemed the contractor’s (s.89). Employers insured with a licensee (for example Rand Mutual or FEM) report to the licensee; employers individually liable carry the claim themselves (s.84). Domestic employees are covered (codifying Mahlangu v Minister of Labour, CC, 2020). Accidents or diseases from 27 April 1994 to 22 January 2026 must be reported by 23 January 2029 (Amendment Act s.63; Prescription Regs reg 2). Confirm the employer and insurer at intake, because it decides who reports and to whom.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: COIDA Administrator (CA); Line Manager or Supervisor (LM); Health and Safety Officer or Representative (HSE); Employee Health and Wellness Representative (EHW, appointed under RRR Regs reg 3); HR Manager (HR); Payroll (PAY); Legal Adviser (LA); Senior Sign-off (SSO); Board, Risk or Social and Ethics Committee (BOARD). External: Compensation Fund or Commissioner (CF); licensee (LIC); Fund Rehabilitation Case Manager (CM); treating medical practitioner (MP); COIDA inspector (INSP).

intro: Phase 0 has no case trigger: it must be in place before the first accident, because if an employer is unregistered, or has not paid its assessment, when an accident happens, the Commissioner may impose a penalty equal to the full compensation payable for that accident (s.87(2)(a)), subject to waiver or instalments (s.87(2)(b)). notes.heading: Employee side of Phase 0
notes.text: Nothing is owed by an employee yet, but their later duties depend on this phase: an employee who has not been told how to report cannot be expected to report well. Inspectors may themselves advise employees of their rights and obligations (Ch XA Regs reg 2(2)).

stages.title: Phase 1 — Accident and immediate response
intro: The 7-day clock starts on the day the employer receives notice of the accident or learns of it in some other way. Day 0 is the day any supervisor or manager first knows; day 1 is the next calendar day.

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Report the accident to the employer as soon as possible (s.38(1)). For a disease, give written notice to the employer, or the last employer, as soon as possible after it begins; the employee may also notify the Commissioner (s.68(1)). Furnish the information and documents prescribed or requested (s.41(1)).

stages.title: Phase 2 — Report to the Commissioner and build the claim
intro: By day 7 for an accident, and day 14 for a disease, the Commissioner (or licensee) must have the employer’s report. Report even where work-relatedness is doubtful: the Commissioner inquires and determines liability (s.40(1)).

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Complete and sign W.Cl.3 or W.Cl.14; furnish documents (s.41(1)); attend any medical examination required (s.42). If the employee obtains a medical report at their own cost and the Commissioner accepts it, the Commissioner must reimburse it in full (s.41(3)).

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: CA → Fund or licensee (reports). CA → treating practitioner (claim details). MP → Fund (first medical report). PAY → CA (earnings). CA → TES or contractor employer.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Failure to report within 7 days “in the prescribed manner” allows the Commissioner to impose a penalty equal to the full compensation payable plus interest from the date of the accident (s.39(8)), separately from the 10% penalty in s.39(6). For a serious injury this is the most expensive failure in the flow. A late report is still better than none: submit it with a short explanation.

stages.title: Phase 3 — Liability, temporary disablement and medical care
intro: While the Commissioner decides liability, the employer carries the first three months of temporary total disablement (TTD) pay, and the employee’s treatment must not stall.

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Submit to medical examination and, if required, examination for rehabilitation (s.42(1), (1A)); follow treatment; provide medical certificates for absence.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: CA ↔ Fund (inquiry and decision). PAY → employee (TTD). CA → LA (objection or variation). MP → Fund (progress reports).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Failing to pay the first three months of TTD attracts a penalty equal to double the full three months’ compensation plus interest (s.47(3)(c)). Where the disablement lasts more than 3 days, pay while liability is pending, and reclaim when the TTD period ends. If liability is rejected, the Fund will not reimburse what was paid: follow the rejected branch at 3.6, and never recover the advance by deduction without the employee’s written consent (BCEA s.34).

source.section: §06 Phase 3 — Liability, temporary disablement and medical care

steps.title: No deductions
steps.action: Never deduct COIDA costs, assessments or any amount the employer must pay under the Act from pay, or recover them from the employee. Sick leave may lawfully apply only to periods for which no compensation is payable (absences of 3 days or less, or claims the Commissioner rejects). GBS policy (BP): grant special IOD leave for these periods so the employee is not worse off; do not debit IOD absence to annual leave.

s.68(2) allows 14 days. The Integrated Policy has this right. Keep 7 days only as a BP target and label it.

Incapacity Hearing Notice, Outcome Retention and Dismissal Letter 1.0; RRR Dismissal Notification; IRP 1.0

Schedule 8 was repealed on 4 September 2025. Cite the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294), Part F. Baseline 2.0’s reference to “Section 2.15” of the Code should be checked against the gazetted numbering.
Hearing notice of “minimum 10 working days as required by the Code”
We found no fixed number of days in the Code; it requires reasonable time to prepare. Present 10 working days as BP.
“Compliance notice … normally 14 days, extendable once”; “employers have 14 days to comply”; “the Inspector may apply to the Labour Court”
Baseline 2.0 Policy 9; Toolkit 11; 2026 Guide and slides

The Act uses “compliance order”; the compliance period is the one stated in the order (s.93F(2)(c), (4)). The 14 days in the Chapter XA Regulations is notice to make representations or of a planned inspection, extendable by 14 days. Only the Commissioner applies to the Labour Court (s.93G).
Fund and Chief Inspector notified only after dismissal
Baseline 2.0 Policy 4.1, 6 (step 12), Template 15; RRR Dismissal Notification

Reg 10(1)(n) also requires notice to the Fund or licensee of the intention to dismiss or reduce remuneration. Add F22. Reg 10(1)(o) separately requires written notice of resumption or inability to retain.
s.64 as substituted imposes an administrative penalty and a direction to repay; it is no longer an offence.
Late reporting penalty: “full compensation amount plus interest, plus 10% of declared earnings”

These are separate powers: s.39(6) (10% of annual earnings), s.39(8) (full compensation plus interest). The “10% plus interest on declared earnings” is s.40(4), for failing the inquiry duties. The base of the 10% is unclear.
Claim window “extended from 12 months to 3 years”
s.44 (lapse) is now 3 years, but s.43 (lodging) still says 12 months. Advise employees to lodge within 12 months; the Prescription Regulations may cure late claims.
30 years applies to RRR reports (reg 10(1)(d)). The earnings register is 5 years (s.81(2)). Longer retention of claim files is a policy choice that must be justified under POPIA s.14.
One “Annual RRTW report to Compensation Fund (Section 85)”
Two different items: mandatory annual reporting data on enrolled cases (reg 10(1)(b)) and an optional s.85 rebate report (reg 12(2)).
OHS Annexure 1 submitted “immediately”; internal target 24 hours

Annexure 1 is not sent to the Department. Immediate telephone or e-mail notice to the provincial director is required for death, unconsciousness, loss of a limb or a major incident (GAR reg 8). The s.24 report goes to the provincial director on W.Cl.2 (W.Cl.1 for a disease) within 7 days (GAR reg 8). Annexure 1 is the internal incident record, completed and investigated within 7 days and kept at least 3 years (GAR reg 9). Keep the 24-hour internal target as BP.
Earnings register at least 5 years after the last entry (s.81(2), increased from 4).
The Prescription Regulations (reg 3) name W.Cl.1, W.Cl.2, W.Cl.3 and W.Cl.14. Confirm current numbering on the Fund’s system.

intro: Paragraph (c) of Proclamation 306 of 2026 lists “19(a) and (b), 20(c), 28(c), 36(1), 50(3), 52, 54(1) and (2)” without saying whether these are sections of the Amendment Act or of COIDA. Section 28 of the Amendment Act has no paragraph (c) of its own, and section 52 amends s.85 (rebates) rather than a penalty provision; s.51 (s.83 penalties) may have been intended.
The 10% penalties in ss.39(6), 40(4), 81(3) and 87 do not identify the earnings or assessment base (all employees, or the injured employee only).
s.81(3) still says an employer “shall be guilty of an offence and be liable to a penalty”, although s.99 was substituted to move to administrative penalties.
s.99 refers to penalties “specified in” ss.68 and 82, but neither section was amended to specify one. Check the consolidated text.
s.43 (12 months to lodge) was not aligned with substituted s.44 (3-year lapse).
“Financial year” in s.1 now runs from 1 April to 31 March, but the maximum-earnings notice (GN 3910) still runs the assessment year from 1 March to 28 February.
s.1(g) (the Income Tax Act definition of “earnings”) has not commenced, so payroll must keep calculating compensation on the old definition.

The RRR Regulations number two regulations as 4 and their table of contents omits regulation 10. The Chapter XA Regulations refer to a “regulation 5 above” that does not exist, to “sub-regulations (a) and (b)”, and contain a paragraph numbered 3.4 under regulation 4.
RRR Regs reg 10(1)(m) requires dismissals to be reported to “the Chief Inspector”, a term COIDA does not define; no form, address or time limit is prescribed.

Third-Party Regs reg 3(3) gives the Commissioner 60 working days to decide, but reg 3(8) deems an application rejected after 60 days. The annual registration window (1 March to 30 June) does not match the six-month deadline in s.73(4)(b), which ended on 23 July 2026.

Notice 7349 (Schedule 4) is framed as a notice of intention with 60 days for comment, yet states that it applies from 1 April 2026. A final notice should be confirmed. Until then, apply the Schedule 4 minimum and maximum in the latest final notice; adopt the Notice 7349 figures (max R41 750; min R5 848) only once confirmed, and adjust retrospectively if required.
The Fund’s printed forms (for example W.Cl.2 directions) still warn that late reporting is an “offence” and refer to the Director-General and mutual associations.

Open verification points (moved here from the body in v1.1): the consequence of refusing a s.42 examination; the commencement of s.83(6)(b) and s.87(3) (23 January 2026 on the published list, subject to issue 1); RRR Regs paragraph references (reg 10(1)(d), (m), (n) and others) against GG 54273; whether a final Schedule 4 notice has been gazetted; and whether the Amendment Act changed the s.56(3) lodging period (24 months, extendable by 12).
